content.text: I was to add tritium or hydrogen isotope diffusivities, solubilities, and permeation properties in Li2O rceramic materials. Make a /plan to do this knowing that I want you to review the existing literature extensively for properties, then create a material property class named TritiumTransportPropertiesLi2O that contains the different properties with Enums for each of the options (NameAuthorYear as names of the enum options). The class should have return the properties and a warning, an error, or ignore it (depending on user preference) if the model is used outside its range. The class should support both AD and non AD and should support models that can sometimes only depend on temeprature, or temperature and irradiation level and other parameters suck as porosity, etc. - as relevant. ALso create a the documentation for these models. They should list the models, provide their range of validity, and have graphs that plot all the relevant models together. The graphs should be generated by a python script. Also generate tests and gold files for all of the models to ensure that we cover them all and ensure proper implementation. Be very careful in your literature search to avoid hallucination, as a critical agent wil provide an adverserial review of the work.

Need the GitHub issue number for this session before I implement anything. Reply with `#<number>` and I’ll execute against that issue.

The repo-specific plan is:

1. Literature phase first, with a hard provenance gate.
   I will build a source matrix for Li2O hydrogen-isotope transport from primary literature only, covering diffusivity, solubility, and permeability/permeation correlations, exact equations, fitted coefficients, units, isotope identity, validity ranges, and independent variables such as temperature, irradiation dose/flux, porosity, density, stoichiometry, grain size, or defect state.
   Any model not traceable to a primary source, or only loosely summarized in a secondary source, will not be implemented.
   I also want a machine-readable data table in the repo so the equations used in code, docs, plots, and tests come from one checked source of truth rather than hand-copied values in multiple places.

2. Implement one material object plus a helper layer.
   I would add `TritiumTransportPropertiesLi2O` as the public material class and put the literature-specific math and metadata in a helper file, following the local `PbLi*Material` pattern already present in your worktree.
   The class should expose separate enums such as `diffusivity_model`, `solubility_model`, and `permeability_model`, with enum names in the `NameAuthorYear` form you requested.
   It should return both regular and AD properties from the same object.
   For correctness, I would make the computational kernels templated on scalar type so temperature-only models and temperature-plus-irradiation/porosity/etc. models can share the same implementation while preserving AD derivatives.
   Validity checking should be generalized across all independent variables, with a single user control like `validity_action = ignore|warning|error`.

3. Keep the interface explicit about model dependencies.
   `temperature` will be required.
   Other inputs such as irradiation level, porosity, density, Li/O ratio, or microstructural state should be optional at the object level but required when a selected model depends on them.
   If a user selects a model that needs a variable they did not supply, that should be a `paramError`, not a silent fallback.
   If the literature only supports permeability as a derived quantity from implemented diffusivity and solubility models, I would make that explicit in both the code and docs rather than presenting it as a direct independent fit.

4. Test every implemented branch, not just the object once.
   I would create a dedicated module such as `test/tests/li2o_transport_properties/`.
   Tests should cover every enum option for diffusivity, solubility, and permeability, plus `ignore`, `warning`, and `error` validity actions, plus AD/non-AD consistency.
   The simplest robust pattern is a tiny one-element input that evaluates the material properties and writes CSV/Exodus outputs for gold comparison.
   For out-of-range behavior, I would add explicit tests for warning emission and hard failure.
   Since this work touches `.C`, `.h`, and `test/tests/`, I would then run only the affected module with `./run_tests -j<N> --re li2o_transport_properties`.

5. Document from the same source matrix.
   I would add [TritiumTransportPropertiesLi2O.md](/Users/simopa/projects/tmap8/doc/content/source/materials/TritiumTransportPropertiesLi2O.md) in the existing MooseDocs material style.
   The page should include:
   a complete model table,
   exact implemented equations,
   original source citations,
   range of validity for every model,
   notes on isotope and microstructure assumptions,
   and explicit statements about any derived permeability models.

6. Generate comparison plots with Python.
   I would add a plotting script in the test/doc area and use MooseDocs `!media`, matching the existing documentation pattern.
   The figures should separate property families cleanly: diffusivity, solubility, and permeability.
   For multidimensional models, the plots should use fixed representative slices that are documented on the page, for example temperature sweeps at selected porosities or irradiation levels.
   I also want the plots to mark the literature validity range visually so out-of-range extrapolations are obvious.

7. Preserve traceability for adversarial review.
   I would update the bibliography with every implemented paper.
   I would keep each enum mapped to a single source entry and a single equation block.
   I would avoid “best guess” conversions by recording the original reported units and the exact conversion used in code/tests/docs.
   If the literature is contradictory, I would document the conflict and either implement both models separately or stop and ask you to choose.

One design adjustment I recommend up front: use one public class, but not one monolithic function body. A helper-backed design with shared metadata is the safest way to support AD, range checks, plotting, docs, and exhaustive tests without duplicating equations.

Send the GitHub issue number and I’ll move from planning into the literature triage and implementation pass.
#419 is the issue number

Issue `#419` is recorded for this session.

**Plan**
1. Literature audit.
   I will collect primary-source Li2O hydrogen-isotope transport models only, then build a checked evidence table with: property type, exact equation, coefficient values, units as published, isotope, independent variables, validity range, and any stated microstructure or irradiation assumptions.
   Secondary reviews can help discover papers, but no model will be implemented unless I verify it against the original source.

2. Model selection and normalization.
   I will separate the literature into:
   `diffusivity` models,
   `solubility` models,
   `permeability/permeation` models.
   For each one I will determine whether it is:
   temperature-only,
   temperature plus irradiation,
   temperature plus porosity/density/stoichiometry,
   or derived from other properties rather than directly fit.
   I will also resolve unit conversions into TMAP8’s expected property forms and note any ambiguity before coding.

3. Class design.
   I will implement a single material class:
   `TritiumTransportPropertiesLi2O`
   with enum parameters like:
   `diffusivity_model`,
   `solubility_model`,
   `permeability_model`.
   Enum entries will use the `NameAuthorYear` form you requested.
   The object will publish both regular and AD properties from the same class.

4. Validity handling.
   I will add per-model metadata for allowed ranges and required inputs.
   The material will support a user-controlled policy such as:
   `validity_action = ignore|warning|error`
   and apply it consistently for temperature and any other required variables like irradiation level or porosity.
   Missing required inputs for a selected model will be hard input errors.

5. Helper architecture.
   I will keep the public class thin and move equations plus metadata into a helper layer, following the same general pattern as the local `PbLi*Material` work already in your tree.
   That keeps one source of truth for:
   equations,
   validity ranges,
   citations,
   plot generation inputs,
   and test expectations.

6. Documentation.
   I will add a MooseDocs page for the class under `doc/content/source/materials/`.
   It will include:
   implemented models,
   exact implemented equations,
   validity ranges,
   required parameters,
   notes on isotope/material-state assumptions,
   and source citations.
   It will also include combined comparison plots for all relevant models.

7. Plot script.
   I will add a Python script that generates the documentation figures.
   The script will read the same model definitions used for implementation where practical, or a single checked data table if direct code reuse is awkward.
   For multidimensional models, the plots will use clearly labeled slices, for example fixed porosity or fixed irradiation levels.

8. Tests and gold files.
   I will create a dedicated test module, likely `test/tests/li2o_transport_properties/`.
   Coverage will include:
   every diffusivity enum,
   every solubility enum,
   every permeability enum,
   AD vs non-AD consistency,
   validity `warning`,
   validity `error`,
   validity `ignore`,
   and any derived-property branches.
   Gold files will be generated for the property outputs and for documentation plot generation where appropriate.

9. Verification workflow.
   Because this adds `.C`, `.h`, docs, and `test/tests/`, I would verify with the affected module only:
   `./run_tests -j<N> --re li2o_transport_properties`
   If `./run_tests` or `./tmap8-opt` errors, I’ll stop and ask, per repo instructions.

10. Deliverable order.
   I would execute in this order:
   literature matrix,
   final model shortlist,
   helper + material implementation,
   tests,
   plot script,
   docs,
   focused test run,
   then commit(s) tied to `#419`.

One important constraint: if the literature is sparse or conflicting for Li2O solubility or permeability, I will not infer missing correlations. I’ll either implement only the defensible subset or stop and surface the gap explicitly.

simulation_time = '${units 40 s}'
P1 = '${units 1 Pa}'
R = '${units 8.31446261815324 J/K/mol}' # from PhysicalConstants
T = '${units 303 K}'
N_a = '${units 6.02214076e23 at/mol}' # from PhysicalConstants
Q = '${units 0.1 m^3/s }'
V2 = '${units 1 m^3}'
V3 = '${units 1 m^3}'
Q_by_V2 = '${fparse Q / V2}'
Q_by_V3 = '${fparse Q / V3}'

[Mesh]
    type = GeneratedMesh
    dim = 1
[]

[Variables]
    [P2]
    []
    [P3]
    []
[]
[AuxVariables]
    [P1]
        initial_condition = ${P1}
    []
[]

[Kernels]
    # Equation for enclosure P2
    [timeDerivative_P2]
        type = ADTimeDerivative
        variable = P2
    []
    [MatReaction_P2_P1_influx]
        type = ADMatReaction
        variable = P2
        v = 'P1'
        reaction_rate = ${Q_by_V2}
    []
    [MatReaction_P2_P3_outflux]
        type = ADMatReaction
        variable = P2
        reaction_rate = -${Q_by_V2}
    []

    # Equation for enclosure P3
    [timeDerivative_P3]
        type = ADTimeDerivative
        variable = P3
    []
    [MatReaction_P3_P2_influx]
        type = ADMatReaction
        variable = P3
        v = 'P2'
        reaction_rate = ${Q_by_V3}
    []
    [MatReaction_P3_P3_outflux]
        type = ADMatReaction
        variable = P3
        reaction_rate = -${Q_by_V3}
    []
[]

[Materials]
    [C2]
        type = ParsedMaterial
        coupled_variables = 'P2'
        property_name = 'C2'
        expression = 'P2*${N_a}/(${R}*${T})'
    []
    [C3]
        type = ParsedMaterial
        coupled_variables = 'P3'
        property_name = 'C3'
        expression = 'P3*${N_a}/(${R}*${T})'
    []
[]

[Postprocessors]
    [P2_value]
        type = ElementAverageValue
        variable = P2
        execute_on = 'INITIAL TIMESTEP_END'
    []
    [P3_value]
        type = ElementAverageValue
        variable = P3
        execute_on = 'INITIAL TIMESTEP_END'
    []
    [C2_value]
        type = ElementAverageMaterialProperty
        mat_prop = C2
        execute_on = 'INITIAL TIMESTEP_END'
    []
    [C3_value]
        type = ElementAverageMaterialProperty
        mat_prop = C3
        execute_on = 'INITIAL TIMESTEP_END'
    []
[]

[Executioner]
    type = Transient
    scheme = bdf2
    solve_type = 'NEWTON'
    petsc_options_iname = '-pc_type'
    petsc_options_value = 'lu'
    automatic_scaling = true
    end_time = '${simulation_time}'
    dt = 0.1
[]

[Outputs]
    csv = true
[]

*** Begin Patch
*** Delete File: test/tests/li2o_transport_materials/li2o_diffusivity_models.i
*** Add File: test/tests/li2o_transport_materials/li2o_diffusivity_models.i
+# Li2O tritium diffusivity material property regression
+# Unit system: SI (temperature in K, diffusivity in m^2/s)
+
+[Mesh]
+  [base_mesh]
+    type = GeneratedMeshGenerator
+    dim = 1
+    nx = 3
+    xmin = 0
+    xmax = 3
+  []
+  [subdomains]
+    type = SubdomainPerElementGenerator
+    input = base_mesh
+    subdomain_ids = '0 1 2'
+  []
+[]
+
+[AuxVariables]
+  [temperature]
+    family = MONOMIAL
+    order = CONSTANT
+  []
+[]
+
+[AuxKernels]
+  [temperature_1]
+    type = ConstantAux
+    variable = temperature
+    block = 0
+    value = 573
+    execute_on = INITIAL
+  []
+  [temperature_2]
+    type = ConstantAux
+    variable = temperature
+    block = 1
+    value = 750
+    execute_on = INITIAL
+  []
+  [temperature_3]
+    type = ConstantAux
+    variable = temperature
+    block = 2
+    value = 950
+    execute_on = INITIAL
+  []
+[]
+
+[Materials]
+  [li2o_diffusivity]
+    type = TritiumDiffusivityLi2O
+    block = '0 1 2'
+    temperature = temperature
+    model = Tanifuji1987
+    property_name = diffusivity
+    ad_property_name = ad_diffusivity
+  []
+[]
+
+[Postprocessors]
+  [value_1]
+    type = ElementAverageMaterialProperty
+    block = 0
+    mat_prop = diffusivity
+    execute_on = INITIAL
+  []
+  [ad_value_1]

$(foreach srcsubdir,$(unity_srcsubdirs_maxdepth),$(eval $(call unity_file_rule,$(call unity_unique_name,$(unity_src_dir),$(APPLICATION_DIR),$(srcsubdir),C),$(shell find $(srcsubdir) \( -type f -o -type l \) -regex "[^\#~]*\.C"),$(srcsubdir),$(unity_src_dir))))

# This creates the whole list of Unity source files so we can use it as a dependency
app_unity_srcfiles := $(foreach srcsubdir,$(unity_srcsubdirs),$(call unity_unique_name,$(unity_src_dir),$(APPLICATION_DIR),$(srcsubdir),C))

# Add to the global list of unity source files
unity_srcfiles += $(app_unity_srcfiles)

# Pick up all of the additional files in the src directory since we're not unity building those
app_non_unity_srcfiles := $(shell find $(non_unity_srcsubdirs) -maxdepth 1 \( -type f -o -type l \) -regex "[^\#~]*\.C" $(find_excludes))

# Override srcfiles
srcfiles    := $(app_unity_srcfiles) $(app_non_unity_srcfiles)
endif



csrcfiles   := $(shell find $(SRC_DIRS) -name "*.c")
fsrcfiles   := $(shell find $(SRC_DIRS) -name "*.f")
f90srcfiles := $(shell find $(SRC_DIRS) -name "*.f90")

# object files
ifeq ($(LIBRARY_SUFFIX),yes)
objects	    := $(patsubst %.C, %_with$(app_LIB_SUFFIX).$(obj-suffix), $(srcfiles))
else
objects	    := $(patsubst %.C, %.$(obj-suffix), $(srcfiles))
endif
cobjects    := $(patsubst %.c, %.$(obj-suffix), $(csrcfiles))
fobjects    := $(patsubst %.f, %.$(obj-suffix), $(fsrcfiles))
f90objects  := $(patsubst %.f90, %.$(obj-suffix), $(f90srcfiles))

app_objects := $(objects) $(cobjects) $(fobjects) $(f90objects) $(ADDITIONAL_APP_OBJECTS)

test_srcfiles    := $(shell find $(TEST_SRC_DIRS) -regex "[^\#~]*\.C" $(find_excludes) 2>/dev/null)
test_csrcfiles   := $(shell find $(TEST_SRC_DIRS) -name "*.c" 2>/dev/null)
test_fsrcfiles   := $(shell find $(TEST_SRC_DIRS) -name "*.f" 2>/dev/null)
test_f90srcfiles := $(shell find $(TEST_SRC_DIRS) -name "*.f90" 2>/dev/null)
ifeq ($(LIBRARY_SUFFIX),yes)
  test_objects:= $(patsubst %.C, %_with$(app_LIB_SUFFIX).$(obj-suffix), $(test_srcfiles))
else
  test_objects:= $(patsubst %.C, %.$(obj-suffix), $(test_srcfiles))
endif

test_cobjects:= $(patsubst %.c, %.$(obj-suffix), $(test_csrcfiles))
test_fobjects:= $(patsubst %.f, %.$(obj-suffix), $(test_fsrcfiles))
test_f90objects:= $(patsubst %.f90, %.$(obj-suffix), $(test_f90srcfiles))
app_test_objects := $(test_objects) $(test_cobjects) $(test_fobjects) $(test_f90objects)

# plugin files
plugfiles   := $(shell find $(PLUGIN_DIR) -regex "[^\#~]*\.C" 2>/dev/null)
cplugfiles  := $(shell find $(PLUGIN_DIR) -name "*.c" 2>/dev/null)
fplugfiles  := $(shell find $(PLUGIN_DIR) -name "*.f" 2>/dev/null)
f90plugfiles:= $(shell find $(PLUGIN_DIR) -name "*.f90" 2>/dev/null)

# plugins
plugins	    := $(patsubst %.C, %-$(METHOD).plugin, $(plugfiles))
plugins	    += $(patsubst %.c, %-$(METHOD).plugin, $(cplugfiles))
plugins	    += $(patsubst %.f, %-$(METHOD).plugin, $(fplugfiles))
plugins	    += $(patsubst %.f90, %-$(METHOD).plugin, $(f90plugfiles))

# main
MAIN_DIR    ?= $(APPLICATION_DIR)/src
main_src    := $(MAIN_DIR)/main.C
main_object := $(patsubst %.C, %.$(obj-suffix), $(main_src))

# all objects that make up an application
all_app_objects := $(app_objects) $(app_test_objects) $(plugins) $(main_object) $(excluded_objects)

# dependency files
app_deps     := $(patsubst %.$(obj-suffix), %.$(obj-suffix).d, $(objects)) \
                $(patsubst %.c, %.$(obj-suffix).d, $(csrcfiles)) \
                $(patsubst %.C, %.$(obj-suffix).d, $(main_src)) \
                $(ADDITIONAL_APP_DEPS)

app_test_deps     := $(patsubst %.$(obj-suffix), %.$(obj-suffix).d, $(test_objects)) \
                $(patsubst %.c, %.$(obj-suffix).d, $(test_csrcfiles))

depend_dirs += $(APPLICATION_DIR)/include
ifneq ($(wildcard $(APPLICATION_DIR)/test/include/*),)
  depend_dirs += $(APPLICATION_DIR)/test/include
endif

# clang static analyzer files
app_analyzer := $(patsubst %.C, %.plist.$(obj-suffix), $(srcfiles))

# library
ifeq ($(LIBRARY_SUFFIX),yes)
  app_LIB     := $(APPLICATION_DIR)/lib/lib$(APPLICATION_NAME)_with$(app_LIB_SUFFIX)-$(METHOD).la
else
  app_LIB     := $(APPLICATION_DIR)/lib/lib$(APPLICATION_NAME)-$(METHOD).la
endif

ifeq ($(LIBRARY_SUFFIX),yes)
  app_test_LIB     := $(APPLICATION_DIR)/test/lib/lib$(APPLICATION_NAME)_with$(app_LIB_SUFFIX)_test-$(METHOD).la
else
  app_test_LIB     := $(APPLICATION_DIR)/test/lib/lib$(APPLICATION_NAME)_test-$(METHOD).la
endif

#
# header symlinks
#
ifeq ($(MOOSE_HEADER_SYMLINKS),true)

include_files	:= $(shell find $(depend_dirs) -regex "[^\#~]*\.[hf]")
all_header_dir := $(APPLICATION_DIR)/build/header_symlinks

# header file links
app_LINK := $(foreach i, $(include_files), $(all_header_dir)/$(notdir $(i)))

$(eval $(call all_header_dir_rule, $(all_header_dir)))
$(call symlink_rules, $(all_header_dir), $(include_files))

# TritiumDiffusivityLi2O

!syntax description /Materials/TritiumDiffusivityLi2O

## Overview

`TritiumDiffusivityLi2O` provides literature-based tritium diffusivity correlations for Li2O and
publishes both a regular and an AD material property from the same object.

The class returns the diffusivity $D$ in m$^2$/s. The literature fits are implemented as reported
and converted internally from cm$^2$/s to m$^2$/s.

!equation
D \; [m^2/s]

## Implemented Models

| Enum | Expression used in TMAP8 | Validity | Notes |
| :- | :- | :- | :- |
| `Ohira1989` | $D = 1.2 \times 10^{-7}\exp(-45.1\times10^3/RT)$ in cm$^2$/s | 600-711 K | Tritium in unirradiated single-crystal Li2O |
| `Tanifuji1987` | $D = 0.116\exp(-101\times10^3/RT)$ in cm$^2$/s | 573-950 K | Tritium release from neutron-irradiated Li2O single-crystal particles |
| `Kurasawa1991` | $D = 2.0 \times 10^{-3}\exp(-81.7\times10^3/RT)$ in cm$^2$/s | 450-820 C | In-situ tritium release interpretation for single-crystal Li2O |
| `Tanaka1988Grain` | $D_g = 1.27 \times 10^{-5}\exp(-54.9\times10^3/RT)$ in cm$^2$/s | 360-600 C | Grain diffusivity from TTTEx polycrystalline Li2O analysis |
| `Tanaka1988GrainBoundary` | $D_{int} = 1.61 \times 10^2\exp(-95.1\times10^3/RT)$ in cm$^2$/s | 360-600 C | Grain-boundary diffusivity from TTTEx polycrystalline Li2O analysis |

The models are not interchangeable descriptions of the same specimen. They reflect different
combinations of:

- single crystal versus polycrystalline interpretation
- irradiated versus unirradiated conditions
- post-irradiation versus in-situ release interpretation
- grain versus grain-boundary meaning for the TTTEx-derived models

The [!param](/Materials/TritiumDiffusivityLi2O/validity_action) parameter controls how TMAP8
responds when a model is evaluated outside its documented temperature range. The supported actions
are `ignore`, `warning`, and `error`.

## Figure

       image_name=li2o_diffusivity_models.png
       style=width:80%;margin-bottom:2%;margin-left:auto;margin-right:auto
       caption=Comparison of the implemented Li2O tritium diffusivity correlations plotted as $\ln(D)$ versus $1000/T$. The top axis shows the corresponding temperature in K.

## Primary Sources

- O'Hira et al. (1989), *Tritium dissolution in and release from Li2O*, DOI `10.1016/S0920-3796(89)80127-9`
- Tanifuji et al. (1987), *Tritium release from neutron-irradiated Li2O: Diffusion in single crystal*, DOI `10.1016/0022-3115(87)90481-8`

# TritiumSolubilityLi2O

!syntax description /Materials/TritiumSolubilityLi2O

## Overview

`TritiumSolubilityLi2O` provides reduced-species tritium solubility models for Li2O and publishes
both a regular and an AD material property from the same object.

The current implementation targets reduced gas-species tritium dissolution behavior represented
with a Sieverts-law type coefficient,

!equation
C = K_s P^{1/2},

where the exact normalization of $K_s$ follows the source-reported coefficient form currently
implemented in TMAP8.

## Modeling Scope

The Li2O literature does not currently support treating all reported chemistry as one scalar solubility model.

Two regimes need to stay distinct:

1. Reduced-species tritium dissolution and transport.
   This is the regime targeted by version 1 of `TritiumSolubilityLi2O`.

2. Oxidized LiOH/LiOT solution chemistry.
   This regime matters for inventory and release, but it is not yet represented here as a source-backed direct scalar property.

## Implemented Models

| Enum | Expression used in TMAP8 | Validity | Notes |
| :- | :- | :- | :- |
| `Ohira1989` | $\log_{10}(K_{s,T}) = 1290/T + 1.14$ | Exact fit range still needs direct PDF confirmation | Reduced-species tritium dissolution in single-crystal Li2O |

## Validity Notes

The O'Hira source provides a source-backed tritium coefficient, but the accessible snippet remains
ambiguous enough in the unit formatting that the implementation should still be checked against the
primary paper for:

- the exact definition of $K_s$
- the exact pressure basis
- the exact temperature range attached to the fit

The current implementation does not apply a hard temperature-limit check for `Ohira1989` because
the exact fit range still needs direct primary-source confirmation. The
[!param](/Materials/TritiumSolubilityLi2O/validity_action) parameter still supports `ignore`,
`warning`, and `error`, but there is currently no numeric range to enforce for this model.

## Figure

The current y-axis still reflects the source-reported coefficient form pending final primary-paper unit normalization.

- O'Hira et al. (1989), *Tritium dissolution in and release from Li2O*, DOI `10.1016/S0920-3796(89)80127-9`
- Katsuta et al. (1983), *Solubility and diffusivity of hydrogen in Li2O*, DOI `10.1016/0022-3115(83)90108-3`
- Tetenbaum et al. (1985), *Investigation of the solubility of LiOH in solid Li2O*, OSTI `5969087`

#!/usr/bin/env python3

from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np


R = 8.31446261815324  # J/mol/K
CM2_TO_M2 = 1.0e-4

SCRIPT_DIR = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
FIG_DIR = SCRIPT_DIR


DIFFUSIVITY_MODELS = {
    "Ohira1989": {
        "prefactor_cm2_s": 1.2e-7,
        "activation_j_mol": 45.1e3,
        "temp_range_k": (600.0, 711.0),
        "label": "Ohira1989, unirradiated single crystal",
    },
    "Tanifuji1987": {
        "prefactor_cm2_s": 0.116,
        "activation_j_mol": 101.0e3,
        "temp_range_k": (573.0, 950.0),
        "label": "Tanifuji1987, neutron-irradiated single crystal",
    },
    "Kurasawa1991": {
        "prefactor_cm2_s": 2.0e-3,
        "activation_j_mol": 81.7e3,
        "temp_range_k": (450.0 + 273.15, 820.0 + 273.15),
        "label": "Kurasawa1991, in-situ single crystal",
    },
    "Tanaka1988Grain": {
        "prefactor_cm2_s": 1.27e-5,
        "activation_j_mol": 54.9e3,
        "temp_range_k": (360.0 + 273.15, 600.0 + 273.15),
        "label": "Tanaka1988Grain, polycrystal grain",
    },
    "Tanaka1988GrainBoundary": {
        "prefactor_cm2_s": 1.61e2,
        "activation_j_mol": 95.1e3,
        "temp_range_k": (360.0 + 273.15, 600.0 + 273.15),
        "label": "Tanaka1988GrainBoundary, polycrystal grain boundary",
    },
}


SOLUBILITY_MODEL = {
    "a": 1290.0,
    "b": 1.14,
    "temp_range_k": (600.0, 711.0),
    "label": "Ohira1989 tritium, provisional range",
}


def diffusivity_m2_s(prefactor_cm2_s: float, activation_j_mol: float, temperature_k: np.ndarray):
    return prefactor_cm2_s * np.exp(-activation_j_mol / (R * temperature_k)) * CM2_TO_M2


def ohira_reported_ks(a: float, b: float, temperature_k: np.ndarray):
    return 10.0 ** (a / temperature_k + b)


def inverse_temperature_axis(temperature_k: np.ndarray):
    return 1000.0 / temperature_k


def temperature_from_inverse_axis(inverse_temperature):
    inverse_temperature = np.asarray(inverse_temperature)
    result = np.full_like(inverse_temperature, np.nan, dtype=float)
    mask = inverse_temperature != 0.0
    result[mask] = 1000.0 / inverse_temperature[mask]
    return result


def inverse_axis_from_temperature(temperature_k):
    temperature_k = np.asarray(temperature_k)
    result = np.full_like(temperature_k, np.nan, dtype=float)
    mask = temperature_k != 0.0
    result[mask] = 1000.0 / temperature_k[mask]
    return result


def add_temperature_top_axis(ax, temperature_ticks_k):
    secax = ax.secondary_xaxis(
        "top", functions=(temperature_from_inverse_axis, inverse_axis_from_temperature)
    )
    secax.set_xlabel("Temperature (K)")
    secax.set_xticks(temperature_ticks_k)
    secax.set_xticklabels([f"{tick:.0f}" for tick in temperature_ticks_k])
    return secax


def apply_axes_style(ax, xlabel: str, ylabel: str, title: str):
    ax.set_xlabel(xlabel)
    ax.set_ylabel(ylabel)
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.grid(which="major", color="0.75", linestyle="--", alpha=0.4)
    ax.grid(which="minor", color="0.9", linestyle=":", alpha=0.4)
    ax.minorticks_on()


def plot_diffusivity():
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.0, 5.5))

    for model in DIFFUSIVITY_MODELS.values():
        t_min, t_max = model["temp_range_k"]
        temperature = np.linspace(t_min, t_max, 250)
        inverse_temperature = inverse_temperature_axis(temperature)
        log_diffusivity = np.log(
            diffusivity_m2_s(
                model["prefactor_cm2_s"], model["activation_j_mol"], temperature
            )
        )
        ax.plot(inverse_temperature, log_diffusivity, linewidth=2.0, label=model["label"])

    apply_axes_style(
        ax,
        r"1000 / Temperature (K$^{-1}$)",
        r"$\ln(D \; [m^2/s])$",
        "Li2O Tritium Diffusivity Models",
    )
    add_temperature_top_axis(ax, [600.0, 700.0, 800.0, 900.0])
    ax.legend(loc="best", fontsize=8)
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig(FIG_DIR / "li2o_diffusivity_models.png", dpi=300, bbox_inches="tight")
    plt.close(fig)


def plot_solubility():
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.0, 5.5))

    t_min, t_max = SOLUBILITY_MODEL["temp_range_k"]
    temperature = np.linspace(t_min, t_max, 250)
    inverse_temperature = inverse_temperature_axis(temperature)
    log_solubility = np.log(
        ohira_reported_ks(SOLUBILITY_MODEL["a"], SOLUBILITY_MODEL["b"], temperature)
    )
    ax.plot(
        inverse_temperature, log_solubility, linewidth=2.0, label=SOLUBILITY_MODEL["label"]
    )

    apply_axes_style(
        ax,
        r"1000 / Temperature (K$^{-1}$)",
        r"$\ln(K_s)$ in reported units",
        "Li2O Reduced-Species Tritium Solubility",
    )
    add_temperature_top_axis(ax, [600.0, 625.0, 650.0, 675.0, 700.0])
    ax.legend(loc="best", fontsize=8)
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig(FIG_DIR / "li2o_solubility_review.png", dpi=300, bbox_inches="tight")
    plt.close(fig)


def main():
    plt.style.use("seaborn-v0_8-whitegrid")
    plot_diffusivity()
    plot_solubility()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from matplotlib import gridspec
import pandas as pd
import os

# Changes working directory to script directory (for consistent MooseDocs usage)
script_folder = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))
os.chdir(script_folder)

# Set path to gold folder based on whether script is run from docs or test directory
if "/tmap8/doc/" in script_folder.lower():
    gold_folder = "../../../../test/tests/val-2j/gold"
else:
    gold_folder = "./gold"

# ============================================================
# Read experimental data
# ============================================================

exp_e = pd.read_csv(os.path.join(gold_folder, "experiment_data_sample_e.csv"))
exp_e_temperature = exp_e["temperature (K)"].values
exp_e_release = exp_e["release_rate (arb)"].values
exp_e_norm = exp_e_release / np.max(np.abs(exp_e_release))


def compute_rmspe(
    sim_temperature, sim_norm, exp_temperature, exp_norm, threshold_fraction=0.05
):
    """Compute the root mean square percentage error (RMSPE) between interpolated
    simulation and experimental data.

    Only points where the experimental value exceeds threshold_fraction of the
    experimental maximum are included.

    Args:
        sim_temperature: simulation temperature array
        sim_norm: normalized simulation release rate
        exp_temperature: experimental temperature array
        exp_norm: normalized experimental release rate
        threshold_fraction: fraction of max experimental value used as filter

    Returns:
        float: RMSPE value in percent
    """
    sim_interp = np.interp(exp_temperature, sim_temperature, sim_norm)
    mask = exp_norm > threshold_fraction * np.max(np.abs(exp_norm))
    rmse = np.sqrt(np.mean((sim_interp[mask] - exp_norm[mask]) ** 2))
    rmspe = rmse * 100.0 / np.mean(np.abs(exp_norm[mask]))
    return rmspe


# ============================================================
# Figure 1: Reference parameters vs experiment
# ============================================================

sim_ref = pd.read_csv(os.path.join(gold_folder, "val-2j_out.csv"))
sim_ref_temperature = sim_ref["temperature_pp"]
sim_ref_release = np.abs(sim_ref["release_rate"])
sim_ref_norm = sim_ref_release / sim_ref_release.max()

rmspe_ref = compute_rmspe(
    sim_ref_temperature, sim_ref_norm, exp_e_temperature, exp_e_norm
)

fig = plt.figure(figsize=[6.5, 5.5])
gs = gridspec.GridSpec(1, 1)
ax = fig.add_subplot(gs[0])

ax.plot(
    sim_ref_temperature,
    sim_ref_norm,
    linestyle="-",
    label="TMAP8",
    color="tab:red",
)
ax.plot(
    exp_e_temperature,
    exp_e_norm,
    marker="o",
    linestyle="None",
    markerfacecolor="none",
    markeredgecolor="k",
    label="Experimental (Sample E)",
)

ax.set_xlabel("Temperature (K)")
ax.set_ylabel("Normalized tritium release rate (-)")
ax.set_xlim(300, 900)
ax.set_ylim(bottom=0)
ax.legend(loc="best")
ax.grid(visible=True, which="major", color="0.65", linestyle="--", alpha=0.3)
ax.minorticks_on()
ax.text(
    0.95,
    0.90,
    f"RMSPE = {rmspe_ref:.2f}%",
    fontweight="bold",
    transform=ax.transAxes,
    ha="right",
)
plt.savefig("val-2j_comparison_sample_e.png", bbox_inches="tight", dpi=300)
plt.close(fig)

# ============================================================
# Figure 2: Optimized parameters vs experiment
# ============================================================

sim_opt = pd.read_csv(
    os.path.join(gold_folder, "val-2j_optimal_bayesian_params_out.csv")
)
sim_opt_temperature = sim_opt["temperature_pp"]
sim_opt_release = np.abs(sim_opt["release_rate"])
sim_opt_norm = sim_opt_release / sim_opt_release.max()

rmspe_opt = compute_rmspe(
    sim_opt_temperature, sim_opt_norm, exp_e_temperature, exp_e_norm
)

fig = plt.figure(figsize=[6.5, 5.5])
gs = gridspec.GridSpec(1, 1)
ax = fig.add_subplot(gs[0])

ax.plot(
    sim_opt_temperature,
    sim_opt_norm,
    linestyle="-",
    label="TMAP8 (optimized)",
    color="tab:red",
)
ax.plot(
    exp_e_temperature,
    exp_e_norm,
    marker="o",
    linestyle="None",
    markerfacecolor="none",
    markeredgecolor="k",
    label="Experimental (Sample E)",
)

ax.set_xlabel("Temperature (K)")
ax.set_ylabel("Normalized tritium release rate (-)")
ax.set_xlim(300, 900)
ax.set_ylim(bottom=0)
ax.legend(loc="best")
ax.grid(visible=True, which="major", color="0.65", linestyle="--", alpha=0.3)
ax.minorticks_on()
ax.text(
    0.95,
    0.90,
    f"RMSPE = {rmspe_opt:.2f}%",
    fontweight="bold",
    transform=ax.transAxes,
    ha="right",
)
plt.savefig("val-2j_comparison_optimized.png", bbox_inches="tight", dpi=300)
plt.close(fig)

# ============================================================
# Figure 2b: Defect density evolution during TDS
# ============================================================

# Analytical solution of defect annihilation ODE:
#   dD/dt = -alpha_anneal * exp(-E_anneal / (kB * T(t))) * D
# with T(t) = 300 + beta*t, beta = 5/60 K/s.
# Solution: D(T)/D0 = exp(-(alpha/beta) * integral_300^T exp(-E/(kB*T')) dT')

kB_J_val = 1.380649e-23  # J/K
E_anneal_J = 0.9 * 1.602176634e-19  # 0.9 eV in Joules
beta = 5.0 / 60.0  # K/s heating rate
T_defect = np.linspace(300, 900, 1000)
dT = T_defect[1] - T_defect[0]

# Integrand: exp(-E_anneal / (kB * T))
integrand = np.exp(-E_anneal_J / (kB_J_val * T_defect))
cumulative_integral = np.cumsum(integrand) * dT  # numerical integration

alpha_anneal_values = [1e1, 1e2, 1e3, 1e4]
colors = ["tab:blue", "tab:red", "tab:green", "tab:orange"]

fig = plt.figure(figsize=[6.5, 5.5])
gs = gridspec.GridSpec(1, 1)
ax = fig.add_subplot(gs[0])

for alpha_val, color in zip(alpha_anneal_values, colors):

    ax.plot(

        color=color,
        label=rf"$\alpha_{{anneal}}$ = 10$^{{{int(np.log10(alpha_val))}}}$ s$^{{-1}}$",

ax.set_xlabel("Temperature (K)")

def get_roots_TMAP4(L, alpha_max, step=0.0001):
    # https://stackoverflow.com/questions/28766692/how-to-find-the-intersection-of-two-graphs/28766902#28766902
    """Gets the roots of alpha = L / tan(alpha)

    Args:
        L (float): parameter L
        alpha_max (float): the maximum alpha to consider
        step (float, optional): the step discretizing alphas.
            The smaller the step, the more accurate the roots.
            Defaults to 0.0001.

    Returns:
        np.array: array of roots
    """
    alphas = np.arange(0, alpha_max, step=step)[1:]
    # Define graph as alphas
    f = alphas
    # Define graph as L / tan(alphas)
    g = L / np.tan(alphas)
    # Find intersections of the two graphs
    idx = np.argwhere(np.diff(np.sign(f - g))).flatten()
    # remove one every other idx
    idx = idx[::2]
    roots = alphas[idx]
    return roots

# TritiumDiffusivityLi2O

!syntax description /Materials/TritiumDiffusivityLi2O

## Overview

`TritiumDiffusivityLi2O` provides literature-based tritium diffusivity correlations for Li2O and
publishes both a regular and an AD material property from the same object.

The class returns the diffusivity $D$ in m$^2$/s. The literature fits are implemented as reported
and stored in the implementation directly in m$^2$/s.

!equation
D \; [m^2/s]

## Implemented Models

| Enum | Expression used in TMAP8 | Property units | Validity range (K) | Notes |
| :- | :- | :- | :- |
| `Ohira1989` | $D = 1.2 \times 10^{-11}\exp(-45.1\times10^3/RT)$ | m$^2$/s | 600-711 | Tritium in unirradiated single-crystal Li2O |
| `Tanifuji1987` | $D = 1.16 \times 10^{-5}\exp(-101\times10^3/RT)$ | m$^2$/s | 573-950 | Tritium release from neutron-irradiated Li2O single-crystal particles |
| `Kurasawa1991` | $D = 2.0 \times 10^{-7}\exp(-81.7\times10^3/RT)$ | m$^2$/s | 723.15-1093.15 | In-situ tritium release interpretation for single-crystal Li2O |
| `Tanaka1988Grain` | $D_g = 1.27 \times 10^{-9}\exp(-54.9\times10^3/RT)$ | m$^2$/s | 633.15-873.15 | Grain diffusivity from TTTEx polycrystalline Li2O analysis |

The models are not interchangeable descriptions of the same specimen. They reflect different
combinations of:

- single crystal versus polycrystalline interpretation
- irradiated versus unirradiated conditions

# TritiumSolubilityLi2O

!syntax description /Materials/TritiumSolubilityLi2O

## Overview

`TritiumSolubilityLi2O` provides reduced-species tritium solubility models for Li2O and publishes
both a regular and an AD material property from the same object.

The current implementation targets reduced gas-species tritium dissolution behavior represented
with a Sieverts-law type coefficient,

!equation
C = K_s P^{1/2},

where the exact normalization of $K_s$ follows the source-reported coefficient form currently
implemented in TMAP8.

## Modeling Scope

The Li2O literature does not currently support treating all reported chemistry as one scalar solubility model.

Two regimes need to stay distinct:

1. Reduced-species tritium dissolution and transport.
   This is the regime targeted by version 1 of `TritiumSolubilityLi2O`.

2. Oxidized LiOH/LiOT solution chemistry.
   This regime matters for inventory and release, but it is not yet represented here as a source-backed direct scalar property.

## Implemented Models

| Enum | Expression used in TMAP8 | Property units | Validity range (K) | Notes |
| :- | :- | :- | :- |
| `Ohira1989` | $\log_{10}(K_{s,T}) = 1290/T + 1.14$ | Source-reported $K_s$ units, pending direct PDF confirmation | Exact fit range still needs direct PDF confirmation | Reduced-species tritium dissolution in single-crystal Li2O |

## Validity Notes

The O'Hira source provides a source-backed tritium coefficient, but the accessible snippet remains
ambiguous enough in the unit formatting that the implementation should still be checked against the
primary paper for:

- the exact definition of $K_s$
- the exact pressure basis
- the exact temperature range attached to the fit

The current implementation does not apply a hard temperature-limit check for `Ohira1989` because
the exact fit range still needs direct primary-source confirmation. The
[!param](/Materials/TritiumSolubilityLi2O/validity_action) parameter still supports `ignore`,
`warning`, and `error`, but there is currently no numeric range to enforce for this model.

# val-2j

# Tritium Thermal Desorption Spectroscopy from Li$_2$TiO$_3$ Solid Breeder

## Case Description

This validation case models tritium thermal desorption spectroscopy (TDS) from neutron-irradiated Li$_2$TiO$_3$ (lithium titanate) crystalline grains, a candidate solid tritium breeding material for Deuterium-Tritium (D-T) fusion reactors. The experimental data and model are from [!cite](kobayashi2015developing).

Li$_2$TiO$_3$ samples were irradiated at the Kyoto University Reactor (KUR) at various neutron fluences. After irradiation, the tritium release behavior was measured by TDS with a heating rate of 5 K/min starting from 300 K using pure helium as the purge gas. The average grain radius was 1.5 $\mu$m.

Sample E (high defect density, $D_{id}$ = $3.384 \times 10^{26}$ m$^{-3}$, corresponding to 0.018 defect/Li$_2$TiO$_3$) is modeled, where tritium release is significantly influenced by trapping at O$^{-}$-centers and defect annihilation.

## Model Description

### Diffusion of Mobile Species

TMAP8 simulates tritium diffusion and trapping in a single spherical grain of Li$_2$TiO$_3$ using 1D spherical coordinates (`coord_type = RSPHERICAL`). The governing equation for mobile tritium concentration $C$ is [!citep](kobayashi2015developing):

\begin{equation} \label{eq:diffusion_trapping}
\frac{\partial C}{\partial t} = D \left( \frac{\partial^2 C}{\partial r^2} + \frac{2}{r} \frac{\partial C}{\partial r} \right) - \frac{\partial C_T}{\partial t},
\end{equation}

where $C_T$ is the concentration of trapped tritium in O$^{-}$-centers and $D$ is the temperature-dependent diffusivity following the Arrhenius law:

\begin{equation} \label{eq:diffusivity}
D = D_0 \exp \left( -\frac{E_d}{k_B T} \right),
\end{equation}

where $D_0$ is the pre-exponential factor, $E_d$ is the activation energy, $k_B$ is the Boltzmann constant, and $T$ is the temperature.

### Defect annihilation

During TDS heating, radiation-induced defect sites undergo first-order annihilation [!citep](kobayashi2015developing):

\begin{equation} \label{eq:annihilation}
\frac{d D_{id}}{dt} = -k_{dp-da} \, D_{id},
\end{equation}

where $D_{id}$ is the defect density and $k_{dp-da}$ is the annihilation rate coefficient. The trap site fraction $\chi$ is related to $D_{id}$. However, the exact relationship is not clearly indicated in [!citep](kobayashi2015developing). Therefore, the initial trap site density is assumed to equal the defect density with $\chi(0)N = D_{id}$ with $N$ as the lattice site density.

$k_{dp-da}$ is described as:

\begin{equation} \label{eq:annihilation_rate}
k_{dp-da} = k_{dp-da,0} \exp \left( -\frac{E_{dp-da}}{k_B T} \right),
\end{equation}

where $k_{dp-da,0}$ and $E_{dp-da}$ are the annihilation prefactor and energy, respectively. Raising the temperature reduces the available trap sites; the trap site fraction $\chi$ decays over time following [eq:annihilation], preventing re-trapping into annihilated sites. This is implemented by solving the annihilation equation self-consistently as an additional variable within the simulation, using a [ReleasingNodalKernel.md].

### Trapping and Detrapping

Only O$^{-}$-center (hydroxyl group) trapping is included in this model. As noted by [!cite](kobayashi2015developing) (p. 26), tritium release controlled by detrapping from F$^+$-centers (oxygen vacancies) occurs near 580 K, which corresponds to the release temperature controlled by the diffusion process itself. Because F$^+$-center detrapping is not rate-limiting relative to diffusion, it does not produce a distinct feature (i.e., peak) in the TDS spectrum, and is therefore excluded from the model.

The trapped concentration $C_T$ evolves according to:

\begin{equation}  \label{eq:trapping}
\frac{\partial C_T}{\partial t} = \alpha_t \frac{C_T^{\text{empty}} C_M}{N} - \alpha_r C_T - k_{dp-da} C_T,
\end{equation}

where $C_T^{\text{empty}} = \chi N - C_T$ is the empty trap concentration.

The trapping and detrapping rate coefficients follow Arrhenius relationships:

\begin{equation} \label{eq:trapping_rate}
\alpha_t = \alpha_{t0} \exp\left(-\frac{\epsilon_t}{k_B T}\right),
\end{equation}

\begin{equation} \label{eq:detrapping_rate}
\alpha_r = \alpha_{r0} \exp\left(-\frac{\epsilon_r}{k_B T}\right),
\end{equation}

where $\alpha_{t0}$ and $\alpha_{r0}$ are pre-factors of trapping and release rate coefficients, and $\epsilon_t$ and $\epsilon_r$ are the trapping and release energies.
The last term in [eq:trapping], $k_{dp-da} C_T$, accounts for the trapped tritium atoms released when full defects are annealed.

### Boundary and initial conditions

- $\partial C / \partial r = 0$ at $r = 0$ (symmetry at grain center)
- $C = 0$ at $r = r_g$ (fast surface release, [!cite](kobayashi2015developing))

The mobile and trapped tritium concentrations are initialized at their local trapping/detrapping equilibrium values at the starting temperature $T_{\text{start}}$ = 300 K. The equilibrium mobile concentration is computed from the balance of trapping and detrapping rates. This avoids an initial transient from any imbalance between trapping and detrapping.
Since the TDS output is normalized to arbitrary units, only the shape of the release curve matters, not the absolute concentrations.

## Results

### Results before optimization

[val-2j_comparison_e] shows the comparison between TMAP8 and the experimental TDS spectrum for Sample E (high defect density). The O$^{-}$-center trapping model with defect annihilation captures the broad release profile. The high detrapping energy of O$^{-}$-centers (1.19 eV) produces a release peak above 650 K that is distinct from the diffusion-controlled release. The defect annihilation mechanism reduces the effective trap density at high temperatures, suppressing re-trapping and allowing tritium to escape more efficiently.

!media comparison_val-2j.py
       image_name=val-2j_comparison_sample_e.png
       style=width:50%;margin-bottom:2%;margin-left:auto;margin-right:auto
       id=val-2j_comparison_e
       caption=Comparison of TMAP8 calculation with the experimental TDS data for Sample E (high defect density).

### Results after optimization

The agreement between the TMAP8 simulation and experimental data can be improved by optimizing the model parameters using the [MOOSE stochastic tools module](https://mooseframework.inl.gov/modules/stochastic_tools/index.html). A Bayesian optimization approach [!citep](DHULIPALA2026102776) was applied to optimize eight key parameters (i.e., four Arrhenius pre-exponential factors (in log$_{10}$ space) and four activation energies for the diffusivity, trapping, releasing, and defect annealing) to better match the experimental TDS curve for Sample E.
As shown in [val-2j_defect_density_evolution], the normalized defect density with the reference annihilation prefactor ($\alpha_{anneal}$ = 10$^2$ s$^{-1}$) remains close to unity throughout the main release region (below ~750 K) and only decreases significantly at higher temperatures where the tritium release flux is decreasing. Larger annihilation prefactors would shift the defect annihilation and the associated tritium release to lower temperatures, but the optimization consistently finds values near the reference.
The optimization used Gaussian Process active learning with Expected Improvement acquisition, running 40 iterations with 5 parallel proposals per iteration.

!media comparison_val-2j.py
       image_name=val-2j_defect_density_evolution.png
       style=width:50%;margin-bottom:2%;margin-left:auto;margin-right:auto
       id=val-2j_defect_density_evolution
       caption=Evolution of the normalized defect density, $D_{id}/D_{id,0}$, during the TDS temperature ramp. As expected, the annihilation temperature strongly depends on $\alpha_{anneal}$.

The objective function evaluates the root mean square percentage error (RMSPE) between the simulated and experimental normalized release rates using a continuous comparison at every simulation timestep. The experimental TDS curve is represented as a piecewise-linear interpolation function, and the RMSPE is accumulated over the full temperature ramp. Low-temperature constraint points (300--475 K) with a small target value penalize parameter sets that produce spurious early release peaks.

[val-2j_optimized_parameters] compares the reference values from [!cite](kobayashi2015developing) with the Bayesian-optimized parameters, along with the parameter ranges used in the optimization.

| $\alpha_{t0}$ | 4.2 $\times 10^{8}$ | 2.21 $\times 10^{7}$ | 10$^{7}$ -- 10$^{10}$ | s$^{-1}$ |
| $\epsilon_t$ | 1.04 | 0.82 | 0.8 -- 1.3 | eV |

# ver-1a

# Depleting Source Problem

## General Case Description

This verification case consists of an enclosure containing a finite concentration of atoms which
are allowed to thermally diffuse through a SiC layer over time. No Soret effects, solubility, or trapping effects are included.

This is one of the original problems introduced in [!cite](longhurst1992verification) for TMAP4 and adapted in [!cite](ambrosek2008verification) for TMAP7. This case has been updated and extended in the context of TMAP8 in [!cite](Simon2025). Note, however, that the verification cases for TMAP4 and TMAP7, although using the exact same setup, use different quantities to verify their implementation (see [ver-1a_comparison_analytical_TMAP4_release_fraction], [ver-1a_comparison_analytical_TMAP7_release_fraction], and [ver-1a_comparison_analytical_TMAP7_flux]). In TMAP8, for completeness, we perform verification on all these quantities and show agreement with analytical solutions from both TMAP4 and TMAP7.

## Case Set up

[ver-1a_schematic] shows a schematic of the ver-1a case, along with an illustration of the quantities used for verification. It consists of an enclosure that is pre-charged with a fixed quantity of tritium in gaseous form and a finite SiC slab. At time t > 0, the tritium is allowed to thermally diffuse through the SiC slab, initially at zero concentration. The surface of the slab in contact with the source is assumed to be in equilibrium with the source enclosure, assuming a temperature-dependent solubility $S$. As a boundary condition, the concentration at the outer surface of the SiC slab is kept at zero for all time. The diffusion of the tritium through the SiC slab is calculated by neglecting Soret and trapping effects. Different aspects of the diffusion are compared against analytical solutions, as described below. The values used to characterize the necessary material properties and the case geometry are provided in [ver-1a_set_up_values].

!media figures/ver-1a_schematic.png
    style=width:50%;margin-bottom:2%;margin-left:auto;margin-right:auto
    id=ver-1a_schematic
    caption= Schematic of the ver-1a case and illustration of the quantities used for verification.

!table id=ver-1a_set_up_values caption=Values of material properties and case geometry with $R$, the gas constant, as defined in [PhysicalConstants](source/utils/TMAP8PhysicalConstants.md).
| Parameter | Description                | Value                                  | Units      |
| --------- | -------------------------- | -------------------------------------- | ---------- |
| $V$       | Enclosure volume           | 5.20e-11                               | m$^3$      |
| $A$       | SiC slab surface area      | 2.16e-6                                | m$^2$      |
| $P_0$     | Initial enclosure pressure | 1e6                                    | Pa         |
| $T$       | Temperature                | 2373                                   | K          |
| $D$       | Tritium diffusivity in SiC | 1.58e-4 $\times \exp(-308000.0/(R*T))$ | m$^2$/2    |
| $S$       | Tritium solubility in SiC  | 7.244e22 / $T$                         | 1/m$^3$/Pa |
| $l$       | Slab thickness             | 3.30e-5                                | m          |

## Verification of the release fraction on the outer surface of the SiC slab (TMAP4)

### Analytical solution

In [!cite](longhurst1992verification), i.e., TMAP4, the verification test focused on the fractional release from the outside of the slab. The analytical solution for this quantity is given by

\begin{equation}
    FR(t) = 1.0 - \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{2\ L \sec (\alpha_{n}) \exp\left(-\alpha_{n}^2[D t/l^{2}]\right)}{L(L+1) + \alpha_n^{2}},
\end{equation}

where

\begin{equation}
    L = \frac{lA}{V \phi}
\end{equation}
with
\begin{equation}
    \phi = \frac{\text{source concentration}}{\text{layer concentration}} = \frac{1}{S k_b T},
\end{equation}

where the "source concentration" is the concentration in the enclosure ($P(t)/k_b/T$), $k_b$ is the Boltzmann constant (as defined in [PhysicalConstants](source/utils/TMAP8PhysicalConstants.md)), and "layer concentration" is the concentration in the slab at the interface with the enclosure ($S P(t)$). $\phi$ is constant in time, and $\alpha_n$ are the roots of

\begin{equation}
    \alpha_n = \frac{L}{\tan \ \alpha_n}.
\end{equation}


!alert warning title=Typo in [!cite](longhurst1992verification)
The expression in Eq. (1) of [!cite](longhurst1992verification) writes $-\alpha_{n}^2(D T/l^{2})$ instead of the correct $-\alpha_{n}^2(D t/l^{2})$ in the exponential. If the interested reader needs convincing, analyze the units in the original report for consistency. Despite this typo, their results are accurate.


### Results

[ver-1a_comparison_analytical_TMAP4_release_fraction] shows the comparison of the TMAP8 calculation and the analytical solution provided in [!cite](longhurst1992verification). There is agreement between the two plots with a root mean square percentage error of RMSPE = 0.19 % for $t \geq 1$ s.

!media comparison_ver-1a.py
       image_name=ver-1a_comparison_analytical_TMAP4_release_fraction.png
       style=width:50%;margin-bottom:2%;margin-left:auto;margin-right:auto
       id=ver-1a_comparison_analytical_TMAP4_release_fraction
       caption=Comparison of TMAP8 calculation with the analytical solution for the release fraction on the outer surface of the SiC slab [!cite](longhurst1992verification).

## Verification of the release fraction on the inner surface of the SiC slab (TMAP7)

### Analytical solution

In [!cite](ambrosek2008verification), i.e., TMAP7, the verification test focuses on the fractional release as determined by the amount of gas release from the enclosure. It is therefore defined as
\begin{equation}
    FR(t) = 1.0 - \frac{P(t)}{P_0},
\end{equation}
where $P(t)$ is the pressure at the surface of the enclosure over time.

To derive $FR(t)$, [!cite](ambrosek2008verification) first references the analytical solution for an analogous heat transfer problem [!cite](Carslaw1959conduction), which provides the solute concentration profile in the membrane as

\begin{equation}
    C(x,t) = 2 S P_0 L' \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{\exp \left(-\alpha_{n}^2 D t\right) \sin (\alpha_{n} x)}{[l(\alpha_{n}^2 + L'^2)+L'] \sin (\alpha_{n} l)},
\end{equation}
where $x=l$ is the position of the surface in contact with the enclosure, and $x=0$ is the position of the outer surface (as defined in [!cite](ambrosek2008verification) - see note below),
\begin{equation}
    L' = \frac{S T A k_b}{V},
\end{equation}
and $\alpha_n$ are the roots of
\begin{equation}
    \alpha_n = \frac{L}{\tan (\alpha_n l)}.
\end{equation}

By linking the concentration on the surface of the slab in contact with the enclosure ($x=l$ as used in [!cite](ambrosek2008verification)) with the pressure of the enclosure, Henry's law provides
\begin{equation}
    P(t) = \frac{C(l,t)}{S} = 2 P_0 L' \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{\exp \left(-\alpha_{n}^2 D t\right)}{l(\alpha_{n}^2 + L'^2)+L'},
\end{equation}
which leads to
\begin{equation}
    FR(t) = 1.0 - \frac{P(t)}{P_0} = 1 - 2 L' \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{\exp \left(-\alpha_{n}^2 D t\right)}{l(\alpha_{n}^2 + L'^2)+L'}.
\end{equation}

!alert warning title=Typos in [!cite](ambrosek2008verification)
1. The units and expression of the solubility provided in [!cite](ambrosek2008verification) have typos. The correct values and units are provided above in [ver-1a_set_up_values]. The value provided in [!cite](ambrosek2008verification) is $S=3.053 \times 10^{\bold{\underline{29}}}$ kg $\cdot$ m $^2$/s$^2$ instead of $S=7.244\times 10^{22} / T = 3.053 \times 10^{\bold{\underline{19}}}$ 1/m$^3$/Pa when $T=2373$ K. The correct value of $S$ is used in the input file decks in [!cite](longhurst1992verification,ambrosek2008verification).
2. The release fraction in [!cite](ambrosek2008verification) is described as $P(t)/P_0$ in their Eq. (5) but is actually plotted as $1-(P(t)/P_0)$ in Figure 1 of that report.
3. Not a typo, per se, but a potential source of confusion for users is that in [!cite](ambrosek2008verification), $x=0$ represents the surface not exposed to the enclosure (where $c=0$), and $x=l$ represents the surface exposed to the enclosure. In the TMAP8 documentation, we have kept this convention to correspond to the TMAP7 case, but note that the TMAP8 input file fixes $x=0$ at the enclosure surface and $x=l$ for the outer surface.

### Results

[ver-1a_comparison_analytical_TMAP7_release_fraction] shows the comparison of the TMAP8 calculation and the analytical solution for release fraction provided in [!cite](ambrosek2008verification). There is agreement between the two plots with a root mean square percentage error of RMSPE = 0.07 % for $t \geq 1$ s.

!media comparison_ver-1a.py
       image_name=ver-1a_comparison_analytical_TMAP7_release_fraction.png
       style=width:50%;margin-bottom:2%;margin-left:auto;margin-right:auto
       id=ver-1a_comparison_analytical_TMAP7_release_fraction
       caption=Comparison of TMAP8 calculation with the analytical solution for the release fraction on the inner surface of the SiC slab [!cite](ambrosek2008verification).

# Li2O Transport Property Shortlist for Issue #419

This note is the pre-implementation review package for the three-class Li2O property set:

- [TritiumDiffusivityLi2O.md]
- [TritiumSolubilityLi2O.md]
- [TritiumPermeabilityLi2O.md]

The goal here is narrower than a full breeder-material review: identify Li2O property models that are safe to encode in TMAP8 without inventing coefficients or silently collapsing distinct physical regimes into one parameter.

## Bottom line

The literature supports a first implementation of:

- reduced-species solubility models based on Sieverts-law fits for `H` and `T` from O'Hira et al. (1989), pending one last direct-PDF unit check;
- several tritium diffusivity models for different Li2O states and microstructures;
- derived permeability only, computed as `permeability = diffusivity * reduced_species_solubility`.

The literature does **not** yet support a clean first implementation of:

- a single undifferentiated "Li2O solubility" property that mixes reduced gas dissolution with oxidized LiOH/LiOT chemistry;
- a direct bulk Li2O permeability correlation from a primary source;
- H/D diffusivity correlations from Katsuta et al. (1983) until the exact fitted coefficients are verified from the primary paper itself.

## Proposed modeling boundaries

The Li2O literature splits naturally into two transport chemistries:

1. Reduced-species dissolution and transport.
   This is the Sieverts-law style treatment for hydrogen-isotope gas in Li2O. It is the cleanest basis for a first `solubility` property and for a derived `permeability = D * Ks`.

2. Oxidized-species trapping / solution chemistry.
   This is the LiOH/LiOT / moisture-coupled regime. It is clearly important for inventory and release, but the accessible primary-source text I recovered so far does not yet give a single compact closed-form correlation that I can encode without additional verification.

Because of that split, I recommend that the initial class design **not** pretend there is one universal Li2O solubility law. The first implementation should explicitly target the reduced-species regime in `TritiumSolubilityLi2O`, and document the oxidized/moisture-driven regime as out of scope for version 1 unless and until we recover the exact primary-source equations.

## Recommended object structure

Your requested split is the better API for this literature set.

1. `TritiumDiffusivityLi2O`
   Owns only Li2O diffusivity models.

2. `TritiumSolubilityLi2O`
   Owns only Li2O reduced-species solubility models for the first pass.

3. `TritiumPermeabilityLi2O`
   Owns Li2O permeability models.
   For version 1, this should at least support a derived option that combines a selected diffusivity model and a selected solubility model internally.

This split is preferable because the literature coverage is asymmetric:

- diffusivity has several source-backed tritium models;
- solubility has a narrower source-backed reduced-species subset;
- permeability appears to be derived rather than directly fit for the implementable set.

Separate classes let users combine supported models without forcing one global transport-model choice.

## Recommended initial implementation set

### `TritiumSolubilityLi2O`

1. `Ohira1989`
   Use for reduced-species Sieverts-law dissolution in single-crystal Li2O.
   Source: O'Hira et al., "Tritium dissolution in and release from Li2O" (1989), DOI `10.1016/S0920-3796(89)80127-9`.
   Recovered coefficients from the publisher snippet:
   `log10(Ks_H) = 1271/T + 2.33`
   `log10(Ks_T) = 1290/T + 1.14`
   Important caution:
   the snippet formatting around the units is ambiguous enough that I want one direct PDF check before I encode the exact normalized units in TMAP8.

### `TritiumDiffusivityLi2O`

1. `Ohira1989`
   Tritium in unirradiated single-crystal Li2O:
   `D = 1.2e-7 * exp(-45.1e3/(R*T))` in `cm^2/s`
   Validity recovered from abstract: `600-711 K`

2. `Tanifuji1987`
   Tritium in neutron-irradiated single-crystal Li2O:
   `D = 0.116 * exp(-101e3/(R*T))` in `cm^2/s`
   Validity recovered from abstract: `573-950 K`

3. `Kurasawa1991`
   In-situ tritium release, single-crystal Li2O:
   `D = 2.0e-3 * exp(-81.7e3/(R*T))` in `cm^2/s`
   Validity recovered from abstract: `450-820 C`

4. `Tanaka1988Grain`
   Polycrystalline Li2O grain diffusion from TTTEx:
   `Dg = 1.27e-5 * exp(-54.9e3/(R*T))` in `cm^2/s`
   Validity recovered from abstract: `360-600 C`

5. `Tanaka1988GrainBoundary`
   Polycrystalline Li2O intergranular transport from TTTEx:
   `Dint = 1.61e2 * exp(-95.1e3/(R*T))` in `cm^2/s`
   Validity recovered from abstract: `360-600 C`

### `TritiumPermeabilityLi2O`

1. `Derived`
   No direct bulk Li2O permeability fit has been recovered yet from a primary source.
   The defensible first implementation is a dedicated permeability class with:
   `P = D * Ks`
   with validity equal to the overlap of the selected diffusivity and reduced-species solubility models.
   This preserves flexibility while keeping permeability as a first-class material property in input files.

## Models reviewed but not safe to encode yet

### Katsuta et al. (1983)

Source:
`Solubility and diffusivity of hydrogen in Li2O`, DOI `10.1016/0022-3115(83)90108-3`

Why it matters:

- it is the clearest early H/D Li2O source;
- the abstract confirms H and D solubility/diffusivity measurements in sintered pellets;
- a later modeling paper cites its activation energy of solution as roughly `16-19 kJ/mol`.

Why I do **not** want to encode it yet:

- the exact fitted solubility coefficients are not recoverable from the accessible abstract alone;
- the exact fitted H/D diffusivity coefficients are also not recoverable from the accessible abstract alone;
- using secondary-source back-calculation here would be too fragile for the adversarial review standard you described.

My recommendation:
keep `Katsuta1983` in the shortlist, but do not implement it until the exact primary-source coefficients are verified from the paper itself.

### LiOH / LiOT solution chemistry papers

Examples:

- Tetenbaum et al. (1985), `Investigation of the solubility of LiOH in solid Li2O`
- moisture-coupled release / trapping discussions used later in MISTRAL-type models

Why they matter:

- they appear central to oxidized-species trapping and inventory;
- they explain why different papers report very different effective release behavior.

Why I do **not** want to encode them yet:

- the accessible source text confirms the physics, but I have not yet recovered a single compact code-ready closed-form correlation for direct property evaluation;
- the transport role here may be better represented later as trapping / reaction submodels rather than as a plain scalar "solubility".

## Recommended class interfaces after this review

I recommend three narrow public objects.

### `TritiumDiffusivityLi2O`

- `isotope = H D T`
- `model = ...`
- `validity_action = ignore warning error`

Required coupled inputs for version 1:

- `temperature`

Likely outputs:

- `diffusivity`
- `ad_diffusivity`

### `TritiumSolubilityLi2O`

- `isotope = H D T`
- `model = ...`
- `validity_action = ignore warning error`

Required coupled inputs for version 1:

- `temperature`

Likely outputs:

- `solubility`
- `ad_solubility`

### `TritiumPermeabilityLi2O`

- `isotope = H D T`
- `model = Derived`
- `diffusivity_model = ...`
- `solubility_model = ...`
- `validity_action = ignore warning error`

Required coupled inputs for version 1:

- `temperature`

Likely outputs:

- `permeability`
- `ad_permeability`

For version 1, I recommend that `TritiumPermeabilityLi2O` compute permeability from internally selected diffusivity and solubility models rather than by requiring users to compose external material properties manually. That keeps the interface flexible without making input-file wiring fragile.

I also recommend two metadata booleans or documented notes internally:

- whether a model is single-crystal or polycrystalline;
- whether a model reflects irradiated, in-situ, or unirradiated conditions.

Those are not cosmetic. They are central to the validity logic and to documentation wording.

## Proposed enum names for review

I recommend short enum names keyed to the lead author and year, with separate entries when the physics is meaningfully different.

For `TritiumDiffusivityLi2O`:

- `Ohira1989`
- `Tanifuji1987`
- `Kurasawa1991`
- `Tanaka1988Grain`
- `Tanaka1988GrainBoundary`

For `TritiumSolubilityLi2O`:

- `Ohira1989`

For `TritiumPermeabilityLi2O`:

- `Derived`

If you want stricter uniqueness with longer names, I can expand them to author lists such as `OhiraHayashiOkunoKudo1989`, but the shorter form is easier to use in input files and still tracks directly to a single source in the docs.

## Validity handling implications

Range checking should not be temperature-only. For Li2O, the documentation should state at least:

- crystal vs polycrystal;
- irradiated vs unirradiated;
- post-irradiation vs in-situ;
- grain vs grain-boundary interpretation when relevant.

My recommendation is:

- use hard-coded numeric checks only for variables explicitly given in the paper, like temperature;
- use warning text for qualitative scope conditions, like "single crystal only" or "irradiated powder interpretation".

That avoids fake precision while still preventing silent misuse.

## Recommendation before coding

If you approve this shortlist, I will next do the documentation draft in the same issue folder in a form that mirrors the eventual MooseDocs pages but does not depend on the classes existing yet.

After that I will implement only:

- source-backed reduced-species solubility,
- source-backed diffusivity models,
- derived permeability in a dedicated permeability class,
- validity warnings/errors for numeric ranges and qualitative scope notes.

I will leave `Katsuta1983` and oxidized LiOT/LiOH transport chemistry out of the first code pass unless we recover their exact primary-source equations first.

1. Literature phase first, with a hard provenance gate.

   Validity checking should be generalized across all independent variables, with a single user control like `validity_action = ignore|warning|error`.

   If a user selects a model that needs a variable they did not supply, that should be a `paramError`, not a silent fallback.

# TritiumDiffusivityLi2O

!syntax description /Materials/TritiumDiffusivityLi2O

## Overview

`TritiumDiffusivityLi2O` provides literature-based tritium diffusivity correlations for Li2O and
publishes both a regular and an AD material property from the same object.

The class returns the diffusivity $D$ in m$^2$/s. The literature fits are implemented as reported
and stored in the implementation directly in m$^2$/s.

!equation
D \; [m^2/s]

## Implemented Models

| Enum | Expression used in TMAP8 | Property units | Validity range (K) | Notes |
| :- | :- | :- | :- | :- |
| `Ohira1989` | $D = 1.2 \times 10^{-11}\exp(-45.1\times10^3/RT)$ | m$^2$/s | 600-711 | Tritium in unirradiated single-crystal Li2O |
| `Tanifuji1987` | $D = 1.16 \times 10^{-5}\exp(-101\times10^3/RT)$ | m$^2$/s | 573-950 | Tritium release from neutron-irradiated Li2O single-crystal particles |
| `Kurasawa1991` | $D = 2.0 \times 10^{-7}\exp(-81.7\times10^3/RT)$ | m$^2$/s | 723.15-1093.15 | In-situ tritium release interpretation for single-crystal Li2O |
| `Tanaka1988Grain` | $D_g = 1.27 \times 10^{-9}\exp(-54.9\times10^3/RT)$ | m$^2$/s | 633.15-873.15 | Grain diffusivity from TTTEx polycrystalline Li2O analysis |
| `Tanaka1988GrainBoundary` | $D_{int} = 1.61 \times 10^{-2}\exp(-95.1\times10^3/RT)$ | m$^2$/s | 633.15-873.15 | Grain-boundary diffusivity from TTTEx polycrystalline Li2O analysis |

The models are not interchangeable descriptions of the same specimen. They reflect different
combinations of:

- single crystal versus polycrystalline interpretation
- irradiated versus unirradiated conditions
- post-irradiation versus in-situ release interpretation
- grain versus grain-boundary meaning for the TTTEx-derived models

The [!param](/Materials/TritiumDiffusivityLi2O/validity_action) parameter controls how TMAP8
responds when a model is evaluated outside its documented temperature range. The supported actions
are `ignore`, `warning`, and `error`.

# TritiumSolubilityLi2O

!syntax description /Materials/TritiumSolubilityLi2O

## Overview

`TritiumSolubilityLi2O` provides reduced-species tritium solubility models for Li2O and publishes
both a regular and an AD material property from the same object.

The current implementation targets reduced gas-species tritium dissolution behavior represented
with a Sieverts-law type coefficient,

!equation
C = K_s P^{1/2},

where the exact normalization of $K_s$ follows the source-reported coefficient form currently
implemented in TMAP8.

## Modeling Scope

The Li2O literature does not currently support treating all reported chemistry as one scalar solubility model.

Two regimes need to stay distinct:

1. Reduced-species tritium dissolution and transport.
   This is the regime targeted by version 1 of `TritiumSolubilityLi2O`.

2. Oxidized LiOH/LiOT solution chemistry.
   This regime matters for inventory and release, but it is not yet represented here as a source-backed direct scalar property.

## Implemented Models

| Enum | Expression used in TMAP8 | Property units | Validity range (K) | Notes |
| :- | :- | :- | :- | :- |
| `Ohira1989` | $\log_{10}(K_{s,T}) = 1290/T + 1.14$ | Source-reported $K_s$ units, pending direct PDF confirmation | Exact fit range still needs direct PDF confirmation | Reduced-species tritium dissolution in single-crystal Li2O |

## Validity Notes

The O'Hira source provides a source-backed tritium coefficient, but the accessible snippet remains
ambiguous enough in the unit formatting that the implementation should still be checked against the
primary paper for:

- the exact definition of $K_s$
- the exact pressure basis
- the exact temperature range attached to the fit

The current implementation does not apply a hard temperature-limit check for `Ohira1989` because
the exact fit range still needs direct primary-source confirmation. The
[!param](/Materials/TritiumSolubilityLi2O/validity_action) parameter still supports `ignore`,
`warning`, and `error`, but there is currently no numeric range to enforce for this model.

    return 1000.0 / temperature_k


def temperature_from_inverse_axis(inverse_temperature):
    inverse_temperature = np.asarray(inverse_temperature)
    result = np.full_like(inverse_temperature, np.nan, dtype=float)
    mask = inverse_temperature != 0.0
    result[mask] = 1000.0 / inverse_temperature[mask]
    return result


def inverse_axis_from_temperature(temperature_k):
    temperature_k = np.asarray(temperature_k)
    result = np.full_like(temperature_k, np.nan, dtype=float)
    mask = temperature_k != 0.0
    result[mask] = 1000.0 / temperature_k[mask]
    return result


def add_temperature_top_axis(ax, temperature_ticks_k):
    secax = ax.secondary_xaxis(
        "top", functions=(temperature_from_inverse_axis, inverse_axis_from_temperature)
    )
    secax.set_xlabel("Temperature (K)")
    secax.set_xticks(temperature_ticks_k)
    secax.set_xticklabels([f"{tick:.0f}" for tick in temperature_ticks_k])
    return secax


def apply_axes_style(ax, xlabel: str, ylabel: str, title: str):
    ax.set_xlabel(xlabel)
    ax.set_ylabel(ylabel)
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.grid(visible=True, which="major", color="0.65", linestyle="--", alpha=0.3)
    ax.minorticks_on()


def order_legend_by_reference_y(line_info, reference_temperature_k: float):
    ordered = sorted(
        line_info,
        key=lambda item: np.interp(
            reference_temperature_k, item["temperature_k"], item["y_values"]
        ),
        reverse=True,
    )
    handles = [item["handle"] for item in ordered]
    labels = [item["label"] for item in ordered]
    return handles, labels


def plot_diffusivity():
    fig = plt.figure(figsize=[6.5, 5.5])
    gs = gridspec.GridSpec(1, 1)
    ax = fig.add_subplot(gs[0])
    line_info = []

    for model in DIFFUSIVITY_MODELS.values():
        t_min, t_max = model["temp_range_k"]
        temperature = np.linspace(t_min, t_max, 250)
        inverse_temperature = inverse_temperature_axis(temperature)
        log_diffusivity = np.log(
            diffusivity_m2_s(
                model["prefactor_m2_s"], model["activation_j_mol"], temperature
            )
        )
        (line,) = ax.plot(
            inverse_temperature, log_diffusivity, linewidth=2.0, label=model["label"]
        )
        line_info.append(
            {
                "handle": line,
                "label": model["label"],
                "temperature_k": temperature,
                "y_values": log_diffusivity,
            }
        )

    apply_axes_style(
        ax,
        r"1000 / Temperature (K$^{-1}$)",
        r"$\ln(D \; [m^2/s])$",
        "Li2O Tritium Diffusivity Models",
    )
    add_temperature_top_axis(ax, [600.0, 700.0, 800.0, 900.0])
    handles, labels = order_legend_by_reference_y(line_info, 700.0)
    ax.legend(handles, labels, loc="upper right")
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig(FIG_DIR / "li2o_diffusivity_models.png", dpi=300, bbox_inches="tight")
    plt.close(fig)


def plot_solubility():
    fig = plt.figure(figsize=[6.5, 5.5])
    gs = gridspec.GridSpec(1, 1)
    ax = fig.add_subplot(gs[0])

    t_min, t_max = SOLUBILITY_MODEL["temp_range_k"]
    temperature = np.linspace(t_min, t_max, 250)
    inverse_temperature = inverse_temperature_axis(temperature)
    log_solubility = np.log(
        ohira_reported_ks(SOLUBILITY_MODEL["a"], SOLUBILITY_MODEL["b"], temperature)
    )
    ax.plot(
        inverse_temperature, log_solubility, linewidth=2.0, label=SOLUBILITY_MODEL["label"]
    )

    apply_axes_style(
        ax,
        r"1000 / Temperature (K$^{-1}$)",
        r"$\ln(K_s)$ in reported units",
        "Li2O Reduced-Species Tritium Solubility",
    )
    add_temperature_top_axis(ax, [600.0, 625.0, 650.0, 675.0, 700.0])
    ax.legend(loc="best")
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig(FIG_DIR / "li2o_solubility_review.png", dpi=300, bbox_inches="tight")
    plt.close(fig)


def main():
    apply_validation_style()
    plot_diffusivity()
    plot_solubility()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
